newsitem.title: USA: IPO FOCUS-Carmax lifts IPO price, deal seen hot.
newsitem.headline: IPO FOCUS-Carmax lifts IPO price, deal seen hot.

text.p: CarMax Group, the used-car retailer being carved out of Circuit City Stores Inc, raised the expected price for shares in its initial public offering.

According to documents filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, the price to buy shares in the IPO is now between $18 to $20 each. The 18.86 million shares had previously been expected to price at between $15 and $17 each.
The shares should get a final price tonight, according to lead underwriter Morgan Stanley & Co.
IPO analysts say Wall Street is clamoring for the stock, which could jump after it opens on the NYSE tomorrow.

CarMax plans a massive expansion with the $338.4 million it hopes to raise from the IPO. It currently operates six outlets in the Southeast United States and a vehicle reconditioning center in Orlando, Fla., but plans to have 80 to 90 locations by the end of fiscal 2002, according to its prospectus.

CarMax has set its sights on the highly-fragmented and lucrative used car industry, which had 1995 U.S. sales of $295 billion, according to CarMax's prospectus, nearly four percent of the U.S. gross domestic product.

The locations offer between 400 to 1,200 vehicles each with a clear "no haggle" price policy. Prices are generally $500 to $1,000 below book value, as defined by the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA), CarMax said.
The stores also offer inspection, reconditioning, financing and some retail repair operations, which CarMax also plans to grow in fiscal 1998.
But despite high sales -- up 258 percent in fiscal 1996 to $275.9 million -- CarMax has yet to turn a profit. It also sees a loss for fiscal 1997, in part due to expansion plans.

The company said it expects each location to reach sales and earnings potential after four years' operation and so far, each of its six has shown an operating profit, excluding the Orlando location, which opened only a few months ago.

Cantor Fitzgerald IPO analyst Vince Slavin said institutional investors like the deal, but because a much larger number of shares are being offered, the deal may not show the same first-day gains as smaller market debuts.
"A good sign is a lot of the right players are buying as a keeper, they're not planning to flip the stock," Slavin said.
"Flipping" refers to investors who are able to get in on an IPO at its offering price but quickly sell the stock on its first day for short-term gains.

One risk for CarMax is that it has said it will need "substantial" capital to fund its expansion in addition to the IPO proceeds. Another is looming competition, most notably in the form of Wayne Huizenga's AutoNation USA, owned by Republic Industries Inc, which is gunning for the same market.
